utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom. Welcome back. The witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Sayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Welcome back. Make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth you made yesterday at the beginning of your testimony still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to greet all those present, and may these proceedings end in accordance with God's will and not my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to greet the witness, and I wish her a pleasant stay with us today. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You're welcome. Yesterday we discussed the agreement of the 24th signed by the Muslim army and the VRS. Among other things, it stipulates that all could be evacuated to a territory of their own choosing for as long as the war went on in keeping with the Geneva Conventions. My question is this: Did you know that nowadays, in Srebrenica -- do you know that in Zepa - sorry, not Srebrenica - there are now people living there who had moved out during the war?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was -- I was aware there had been some return of former refugees, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that one of the signatories of that agreement also currently resides in Zepa? He testified here before the Chamber and he stated his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. I just want to make sure that there's no confusion on the record. General Tolimir referred to an agreement signed on the 24th which he said was signed by the Muslim army, so, number one, I'm -- I just want to make sure we're talking about the agreement on the 24th, because I think we're -- we would all be agreed that that was signed by Mr. Torlak. If it's the General's position that he represents the army, then so be it. But I just want to make sure because we've talked about three, possibly four, agreements, one in a meeting on the 19th that was signed by General Smith, the 24th, the 27th, and General Tolimir is now referring to a witness who he is saying lives in Zepa, and I'd be curious to know who that witness is. And we can put it on the record outside the hearing of the present witness, if the Court thinks that's more appropriate, but I'd just like to know who that witness is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you clarify the background of your question? Was it just a mistake or what was it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible that there was a mistake. I believe I said that the Muslim side signed it on the 24th of July, not the Muslim army. In any case, we will clarify who represented the Muslim side when the agreement was signed. It will become clear through further questions. I just wanted to know whether this witness was aware that one of the persons who signed that agreement now resides in Zepa. I didn't want to mention his name, since he appeared here as a protected witness. If Mr. Thayer wishes to do so, we can go into private session and then I can state his first and last name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think this is a good proposal. I know that this person was not a protected witness. He didn't have a pseudonym. But we were all very careful mentioning his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And perhaps we can just save a little bit of time. If it is the witness I think General Tolimir is referring to, a simple transcript cite to the portion of the testimony where this witness allegedly stated that he currently lives in Zepa would be helpful. I'm not aware of any such testimony. So if he has it, I would appreciate it, before this witness answers a question based on that proposition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should first go into private session so that there is no problem with giving the details. Mr. Tolimir, just a moment, we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Madam, yesterday, at transcript page 1975 [sic], lines 16 to 23, you said the following about the meeting of the 25th of July, 1995. I quote: We met with Mr. Torlak because he was a type of main representative. He was introduced to us as the main representative of the population of Zepa, of the Bosniak Muslim population. General Smith was very interested in meeting him so as to be able to discuss things with him and to convey the fact to him that from Zepa we were to go to the Bosnian Presidency to meet with Minister Muratovic and the president. We would be able to directly convey Torlak's concerns to them. Most of the conversation had to do with the exchange of POWs. My question is this: You said that Mr. Torlak acted as a representative. Did he represent the Muslim population and the Presidency as such, or how did he introduce himself during the discussion General Smith had with him?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was introduced to us by General Mladic as one of the members of the Zepa War Presidency, and he at no stage said that he represented the Bosnian military. It was made very clear that he was a civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question is this: During the meeting, did you raise the issue of whether Torlak or some other members of the War Presidency represented the population of Zepa and whether they were in communication with the government in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- we understood from how he had been introduced to us that he was representing the civilian population in Zepa, and I don't recall they -- them being in communication with the government in Sarajevo. Not on the civilian side. I believe -- I believe there was a doctor going on one of the convoys with the wounded into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to mention for the record that the page of the transcript of yesterday's hearing was recorded incorrectly. Page 5, line 23, you are recorded to having said "at transcript page 1975." It is, in fact, page 10975. Just for the record. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: At transcript page 10976, lines 3 to 8, in answer to one of the Prosecutor's questions about General Smith's conversation with Hamdija Torlak you said the following: General Smith tried to gain an impression about the atmosphere and situation in Zepa and its population. At that stage he asked Mr. Torlak whether anyone wished to remain in Zepa. My previous testimony had to do with my clear recollection when I saw a type of disbelief or shock on the face of Mr. Torlak when he heard that question being put to him. Next you said this. The question was whether Mr. Torlak communicated with General Smith about his belief of what was going to happen with anyone who remained. And you answered in lines 12 to 15: Yes, it was clear that any Muslim, any able-bodied Muslim, who remained, would be at the risk of being killed if they remained. Did this part of the conversation have only to do with the able-bodied men or the entire civilian population?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The entire civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In Mr. Torlak's response, did he mention the able-bodied part of the population when responding to General Smith?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did Mr. Torlak say, Yes, it was clear that any able-bodied Muslim man remaining behind would be at the risk being killed? Is this what Mr. Torlak said?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression, my recollection, is that he was speaking under duress.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I heard your opinion. But is what you stated in lines 12 to 15 correct, when you said that his answer was purportedly if any able-bodied Muslim man remained in the enclave would be risking his own death? I quoted you from lines 12 to 15. Do you stand by it or would you deny it now?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forgive me, but I don't have any copy of the transcript in front of me, so I would find it helpful if I could see that. Would that be possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would be possible, technically speaking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yesterday's transcript, page 10976.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lines 15 to 18. Apologies, lines 12 to 15.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. Okay. Thank you. Yes, I stand by lines 12 to 15 of the transcript. It's exactly what I said yesterday. They were repeatedly -- Mr. Torlak asked for the use of helicopters because they did not believe that road transport would be safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know -- I realize you stand by what you said, but did you say yesterday that Mr. Torlak had the able-bodied men in mind when answering? I believe you still haven't provided me with an answer to that.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He -- he did mention that Avdo Palic was in charge of the men of fighting age within the enclave. And when I've said in lines 12 to 14 that they were -- any man of fighting age was at risk, at risk of death were they to remain in the pocket, yes, that is my recollection of our conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since Mr. Torlak, in lines 12 to 15, is not addressing the issue of the civilian population, the disbelief on his face you saw, did it have to do with the men of fighting age or civilian -- of civilians?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you provide your answer then based on what you could read on Mr. Torlak's face?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, what I recall very clearly was the look of shock or disbelief when Generals -- on Mr. Torlak's face when General Smith asked him specifically whether anybody wanted to remain in the pocket. And General Smith did not say whether any men of fighting age wished to remain in the pocket. He said whether anybody wishes to remain in the pocket. I hope that clarifies my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you testified during examination-in-chief and you wanted to say whatever you felt like; is this in addition to what you stated in your statement?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would respectively request that this type of question end now. We don't need this kind of harassment of the witness. We heard some of it yesterday, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- to say that the witness is saying whatever she wants, Mr. President, is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not of your opinion. This witness was present during this conversation. It is not a harassment. It is part of legitimate cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no problems with him asking her questions about what she saw, what she heard, what her opinion is, what she thought somebody was thinking based on the demeanor. Again, my objection is to the disrespect with which that question is asked. Where he characterizes what she said yesterday as saying whatever she felt like. We heard that yesterday, and I think it should end. He should ask questions in an appropriately respectful manner of this witness, the same respect that we ask for every witness that comes before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, Mr. Tolimir put to the witness the following: "Yesterday you testified during examination-in-chief and you wanted to say whatever you felt like; is this in addition to what you stated in your statement?" I don't see any harassment in this wording. Mr. Tolimir, please continue. Or I would like to say, Ms. Sayer, would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't really understand what you mean when you said -- when you asked me if I -- if I said anything that I feel like. I'm doing my best to answer the questions that you have asked me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to thank Mr. Thayer and the witness, Ms. Emma. I will not put any more questions on this topic if anyone feels irritated by them. Could we please have a look at the footage which is Exhibit D108. It was recorded at Boksanica on the 19th of July, 1995. I think Mr. Torlak's there, General Mladic, and Mr. Kulovac. The footage only lasts for 18 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Yes, we can do that immediately. But before we start with that, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we don't want to place any limitations on the questions, substantive questions, that Mr. Tolimir wishes to ask this witness. I want to make that clear. He's threatening to move on to another topic because of what he says he says. If he wants to ask more questions on that topic, that's fine. But again, to use that, to threaten to take his marbles and go home, is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please let this document be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This is D108, a footage from Boksanica where the witness was. We can see some people that the witness met at Boksanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether you can recognise the faces of the people in the still? And since you said you recall being in Zepa, do you recall who the people you talked to were?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, I do recall the people who I talked to. I don't -- I don't recognise all the people in the still that I have on the screen in front of me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And which of them do you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recognise the gentleman on the left-hand side and General Mladic, who is on the right-hand side. I don't really recognise the man in the middle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That would not be a problem to mention the name of the man of the left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honour. I believe the man on the left-hand side to be Mr. Torlak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. And thank you Ms. Emma.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The person in the middle you don't know is the person you met when you were there with General Smith. It is Mr. Kulovac. Perhaps you could recognise him if he had a hat on on this still. They were there as civilian representatives in any case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please play the footage to see what their demands were. It's only 18 seconds long.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw the footage but I'm afraid not the sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that was the sound. We could see that it was the highest possible sound. This witness is Ms. Sayer. Her first name is Emma. I just want to remind you to address her in the appropriate way. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Sayer, could you hear what the people were -- in the still were saying? If not, we can replay it and try to put the volume up a bit.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't hear it very clearly, but I can read the subtitles that are in English at the bottom of the footage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it was that you were able to read in the subtitles?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does anybody wish to stay, and then I did hear General Mladic say, Koliko, how many? And then the two representatives talked about -- about ten families wishing to stay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We could try to play it again because we have now another size. If you wish, Mr. Tolimir, that could be possible.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We heard them refer to a full ten families that have remained in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Sayer, did Mr. Torlak say something similar at the meeting with General Smith on the 27th of July, 1995, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't recall him mentioning that there were a number of families that wanted to stay, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show P1979. It's Baxter's report on the situation in Zepa of the 26th of July, 1996. And we're interested in page 4 in Serbian and page 3 in English. Paragraph 10. P1979. Thanks. We have paragraph 10 in English. You can read it. And we'll have it shortly in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is what Mr. Baxter had to say, and I'm quoting from paragraph 10: "General Smith asked whether anybody wished to remain in the enclave. Torlak replied that the general atmosphere was that everyone wanted to leave on the grounds of security. He had no details about the handing over of weapons and said he would have to check with Avdo Palic. Torlak stated that if the men in the enclave were more confident that the Bosnian government would agree to the POW exchange, the mood of fear would immediately alter." This is my question: Was basically the concern that Hamdija Torlak had the issue of security and whether the government in Sarajevo would agree to a prisoner exchange? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did -- he did speak about the -- that nobody wanted to stay in the pocket of Zepa on the grounds of security. And it was clear that there was concern about whether the Bosnian Presidency would agree to an all-for-all prisoner of war exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was his main concern whether an exchange would be agreed to and whether they would be able to leave Zepa, since they had no intention of staying there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that he -- he was very concerned about whether the prisoner of war exchange would happen and that that question mark was causing a lot of uncertainty and fear amongst the men of fighting age within the pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was his fear down to what the Bosnian government would decide with respect to the exchange or down to what the Serbian side might decide to do with the prisoners? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that he was concerned that the prisoner exchange would not be agreed. And the implication was then that the men of fighting age, you know, would -- would be at grave risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the answer you've given me, I have to repeat what Mr. Torlak said to General Smith so that both you and the Trial Chamber and all of us can have a look, including the Prosecution. And I repeat. Torlak stated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Tolimir, Mr. Tolimir, this is a waste of time. You have read it to the witness. We have -- everybody in the courtroom has it on the screen. There's no need just to repeat. You may put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question was: Was he expressing his concerns about the exchange or about the position that the government would take in relation to the prisoners of war exchange, which would ultimately lead to their release to freedom? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that the concerns focussed on the -- on -- on the prisoner exchange, on the fact that if a prisoner exchange was not agreed, the men of fighting age within the enclave would -- would be at risk. I'm not sure I quite captured what you meant about the position of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I was giving you my understanding of Mr. Torlak's words. I was basing my question on what he said to General Smith. I can't construe his words in any way. My question for you was: Were his concerns about what the Serbian army would have to say about the exchange or what the Bosnian government's position on that would be? Did you know at all -- at all if he was able to know what the VRS position with regard to the exchange was?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To clarify, my recollection is that Mr. Torlak was concerned about the Bosnian Presidency's response to the suggestion for the prisoner exchange. And I -- I can't speak to the question, the supplementary, that you've asked about the VRS position. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sayer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show Exhibit D54. This is a letter sent by Mr. Izetbegovic to Mehmed Hajric on the 19th of July, 1995, wherein he states, and I'm quoting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You have it there in English now. I'm quoting from paragraph 3 of the letter sent by Alija Izetbegovic to Effendi Mehmed Hajric, president of the War Presidency of Zepa on the 19th of July, 1995. You'll see his signature at the bottom later on. I'm quoting from paragraph 3: "My plan is to move out as many civilians as possible. All of them, if possible. The troops stay on and continue to resist. We will do everything in our power to help you by supplying materiel and technical equipment, volunteers, and offensive action in your direction. I do believe this is going ahead today. If we do not succeed in this, you will try to push on along those roads. You know which. But this time without the burden of women and children who would, in the meantime, be pulled out." First of all, were you present during the talks Alija Izetbegovic had with General Smith on these issues? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in my testimony yesterday, I was present at the meeting very late in the evening, started at 2340 hours and after our first day or afternoon in Zepa with President Izetbegovic. I was present at that meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you give us the date of that meeting, please, for the record? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the 25th of -- of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So it happened seven days before the letter he sent to Zepa. So did he, seven days later, in the presence of General Smith, present his view of the situation in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may be a little confused but the transcript I have in front of me says that it happened seven days before the letter he sent to Zepa. Is that just a mistranslation? Because ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't know, but it seems to be wrong.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The meeting you attended --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- took place on the 25th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's just the other way around.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which is -- the other way, which is after - thank you - which is after this letter. They -- we had a long conversation between General Smith and President Izetbegovic, and also the two ministers were there, Muratovic and Masovic. And there was a long exchange of information with General Smith updating the president on what had happened during our visit to check-point 2 in that -- that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you remember what he had told you about the evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa and the remaining behind of the able-bodied men? Did he make any points on that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minister Muratovic was very keen to know from General Smith whether the Armija forces, particularly Avdo Palic was mentioned at this point, had signed the agreement of the 24th of July that had been signed by the Zepa War Presidency, and he led the questioning of General Smith about that particular element.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday, you testified to the 65 ter document 6072 that was shown to you by the Prosecution. This is the so-called Baxter's report. Can we call it up, please, and specifically item 16 which refers to this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And this is now P1979.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see paragraph 16 where Izetbegovic tells General Smith as follows: "Izetbegovic told General Smith that he expected a new UN resolution in the next few hours enabling UNPROFOR to assume all the arrangements for the evacuation from Zepa and asked him whether he was ready to implement such a resolution." Do you remember this issue, since you were present at the meeting Mr. Baxter is writing about? And, if so, do you recall what it was that Alija Izetbegovic had in mind when he spoke these words to General Smith?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this particular exchange. And President Izetbegovic explained that he had been speaking to a number of different people from different countries, was the impression that he gave, to try to increase support for a new UN resolution that would alter the UNPROFOR mandate to allow us -- to allow UNPROFOR to implement the arrangements for the evacuation from Zepa. My recollection is that General Smith was very clear that, obviously at the time, our existing, our existing mandate, you know, was what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember the date of this particular meeting? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular exchange happened in the very early hours of the -- the 26th of July. So, you know, almost 1.00 in the morning, is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa over by then? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll look at reports speaking to this later on. Let us now look at the rest of paragraph 16, starting from line 4, and I'm quoting: "Muratovic complained that UNPROFOR had assisted the evacuation of Zepa without the permission of the Bosnian government and that UNPROFOR should be responsible for compiling lists of the refugees on the buses, escorting them safely to Kladanj, and comparing the figures and names on arrival in Kladanj." This is my question: Does it follow from this that the operation of evacuating the population from Zepa was conducted with the assistance of UNPROFOR and that these people were on the buses, as Muratovic says? So did you see civilians in Zepa on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This -- this meeting note refers to the 25th, to our experiences in the Zepa on the 25th rather than 26th. And my -- as I mentioned yesterday, my colleague Captain Tom Dibb, who had been down in Zepa town, had seen, you know, civilians down actually in Zepa town. This exchange between Minister Muratovic was very heated. There was quite a lot of tension because Muratovic was very concerned that similar problems with the evacuation of the civilian population in Srebrenica on buses would occur in Zepa, and he -- he really was very keen that UNPROFOR should keep detailed records of every person that got on a bus driven by a Serb out of the Zepa pocket. And that -- I remember the conversation being quite tense.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. But you do see that this is contradictory to what Muratovic had to say. He criticised UNPROFOR for participating in the operation of compiling lists and for matching the lists compiled in Zepa with those compiled in Kladanj. Were you aware of this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forgive me that that is not correct. Muratovic was insisting that UNPROFOR should compile lists of people on the buses and that, you know, it says -- it says quite clearly here "and that UNPROFOR" -- oh, I've touched the screen, I'm sorry, it's gone. Sorry. "And that UNPROFOR should be responsible for compiling lists of the refugees on the buses, escorting them safely to Kladanj, and comparing the figures and names on arrival in Kladanj." And Muratovic's main contention was that that level of detail and UNPROFOR security was not being given to the refugees, and that's what the Bosnian side was so worried about. I hope that clarifies the language that I've used. And I did author this report, and you can see my signature at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at the first sentence of this paragraph or, rather, the first part of this sentence. "Muratovic complained that UNPROFOR had assisted the evacuation of Zepa without the permission of the Bosnian government and that UNPROFOR should be responsible for compiling lists of the refugees on the buses," and only at this point do we have a comma in the sentence. Is that a phrase that is independent or is it dependant on the rest of the sentence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the English text I don't see a comma. Perhaps it's a translation issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, yes. I think my last answer sort of explained that Muratovic was unhappy that we had been in the pocket of Zepa and had observed civilians, you know, preparing for the evacuation of a civilian population from the Zepa pocket but that we hadn't -- UNPROFOR hadn't taken, you know, the full responsibility for it. It was a Bosnian Serb army operation. It was not an operation that UNPROFOR was in any way controlling. So I hope that clarifies, in answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I would like to clarify with you to which comma you were referring. In the B/C/S text or in the English text? I see only a comma after the word "autobusima" in the B/C/S or "refugees on the buses" in the English text. Was that the comma you were referring to or to another? A comma in the beginning of the sentence between the first and the second part would change the meaning. But there is no comma, in my understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I said that a comma came only after "the buses," so whatever is written ahead of the comma relates to that particular clause. In other words, Muratovic complained that UNPROFOR had assisted the evacuation of Zepa and that UNPROFOR should be responsible for compiling lists. So this report refers to a protest that Muratovic lodged with UNPROFOR. Let's see what Alija Izetbegovic had to say further down. Paragraph 16, third line from the bottom: "Izetbegovic thanks General Smith for his help an efforts and said that the government would await the outcome of the new UN resolution and, in the meantime, speak to Dr. Kulovac and continue its efforts through Masovic and the prisoners of war exchange commission."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Do you remember, what was it that Alija Izetbegovic was thanking General Smith for? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Izetbegovic was thanking General Smith for actually going out to the check-point 2 as -- himself, personally, after the morning meeting with General Mladic. And he was thanking him for his personal, you know, feedback from that meeting about the situation on the ground. And also he made reference to the fact that General Smith had sent a headquarters UNPROFOR liaison team with independent communication, of -- the Ukrainian company was there, into Zepa town itself with civil affairs support, and President Izetbegovic was expressing gratitude for the course of action that General Smith had taken in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since General Smith will testify here, he will tell us what it was that he was discussing with Izetbegovic. Therefore, I won't ask you to interpret his opinion. Let's look at D173 in e-court. It is a report drafted by the same people that were referred to. General Smith sent that report to Zepa. Without going back to paragraphs 15 and 16 of this document because they are quite lengthy. Thank you. We see a statement of one of those people by sent by General Smith to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go to page 3. He arrived on the 19th, pursuant to General Smith's orders. Let us go to page 3, please, paragraph 16, and paragraph 17. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is what is stated in paragraph 16. I quote: "We created written lists of the evacuees. And as far as I can recall, we had a separate list for each vehicle. I handed over those lists later, either to UNHCR or someone in UNPROFOR. We also tried to place one UNPROFOR soldier to each vehicle, but I'm not sure if we managed to do it all the time during the evacuation." In paragraph 17 it says: "The evacuation lasted probably three days ..." he arrived on the 19th. And he goes on to say, "or a bit longer. The atmosphere was quite tense throughout, but we managed to get all those people on board who had come to the centre and were willing to go. In my estimate, approximately 7.000 people were evacuated." This was paragraph 16 and 17 of D173. This particular witness testified before you. Can you tell us this: At the time when General Smith was there, when the meeting with Izetbegovic was held, were you able to find any civilians in the enclave of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I testified yesterday, the meeting with Izetbegovic was held on -- in the very early hours of the morning of the 26th and related to the events of the 25th of July. So there were a number of -- when we arrived --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, it would very polite if you could listen to the witness when she is giving you an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. So when we first arrived on that first afternoon, on the 25th, there were a number of vehicles in the area of check-point 2, and that's when we had the opportunity to meet up face to face with the headquarters UNPROFOR liaison team, and specifically Captain Dibb. And I believe that at that stage General Smith did have an opportunity to speak to both Captain Dibb and, I think, the civil affairs teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read this report written by civilian affairs? Did that person send any reports about the evacuation to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally have never seen this piece of witness statement before or my -- my role at the headquarters was not to read the civil affairs reports. So I'm aware that information was transmitted by my colleague Captain Tom Dibb and the civil affairs team throughout their whole time that they were in the Zepa pocket, but I didn't personally read all of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the clarity of the record, this document on the screen in front of us is witness statement of Mr. Joseph of 2005. Were you referring to this statement when you were mentioning a report of civil affairs, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I did have the statement in mind, and I asked the witness whether she ever received reports from Mr. Joseph. I do not dispute that the evacuation took place on 15th, the 16th, and the 17th, but he was in charge of the evacuation and he probably reported on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, that was not my question. I was referring to your question you put to the witness, page 25, line 11. I quote: "Have you read this report written by civilian affairs?" To which report written by civilian affairs were you referring to? Or were you referring to the witness statement of Mr. Joseph? That was the matter I would like to ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I wanted to ask whether she read any reports sent by Edward Joseph as the civil affairs officer. That is to say, any reports sent by UNPROFOR command to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is really a different question now. The witness may answer that. But in the meantime, I would like to see the first page of this witness statement of Mr. Joseph again. It will be on the screen shortly. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. President, I don't think there's any dispute but perhaps General Tolimir misspoke with respect to the dates. We have the 15th, 16th, and 17th. I don't think there's any dispute that we're talking about the 25th, 26th, and 27th of July, just so there's no confusion when we go back to the record later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what we have on the screen is on the head of the ICTY OTP information report. Submitter, Olli Salo; subject, interview with Edward Joseph; date, 9th of February, 2005; witness, personal details. And then we have a witness statement. But your last question was whether the witness read any reports sent by Edward Joseph as the civil affairs officer. Ms. Sayer, could you answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civil affairs reports that I would ordinarily read as part of my role related normally to the Bosnian Muslim or the Bosnian Croat side. So the reports that I read from the UNPROFOR liaison team that was in the Zepa pocket over this period were all coming from Captain Dibb as opposed to Mr. Joseph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I quoted paragraphs 16 and 17 from the statement. Is it clear from those paragraphs that Mr. Joseph also took part in the creation of lists of those who were to be evacuated? And was he also in charge of assigning personnel to escort the buses?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to that. My recollection about the personnel on the buses was that that was the responsibility of the French military contingent of UNPROFOR, as opposed to civil affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not familiar with your tasking, but I just wanted to go back to paragraph 16. Here, it is stated that they created written lists. That means the persons who wrote the report of the evacuees. "And as far as I can recall, we had separate lists for each vehicle. I handed over those lists later, either to the UNHCR or someone in UNPROFOR. We also tried to place one UNPROFOR soldier to each vehicle, but I'm not sure if we managed to do it ... throughout the evacuation." My question is this: Did any civil affairs, UNHCR, and UNPROFOR representatives take part in the evacuation of the civilians from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have referenced yesterday in my testimony, I was aware that this took place actually in Zepa town where I was never present. But from my conversations with Captain Tom Dibb, you may recall from yesterday's testimony that there was quite a significant debate and some tension between the ICRC people and the UNPROFOR people that actually were in the Zepa pocket over -- over the difference sorts of activities that they should undertake or be willing to undertake. So I did not know that there were written lists for each -- each vehicle, for example. But I did know that there was an attempt to put an UNPROFOR person on each of the vehicles. And I remember there being an exchange between General Smith and General Mladic when that hadn't happened, when, you know, UNPROFOR soldiers were forbidden to get on a number of vehicles, and General Smith raised this as a matter of concern with General Mladic. So that's the extent of my knowledge relating to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were UNHCR and UNPROFOR representatives, as well as civilian affair representatives and Mr. Dibb, allowed to evacuate any person from the centre of town and was willing to leave? We can see that in paragraph 16 -- 17. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that an evacuation took place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the VRS had no participation in the checking of IDs, age, and those put on board those vehicles? Not a single person was checked out of the entire civilian population that was to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My -- in yesterday's testimony, I explained that I have seen Captain Tom Dibb on the afternoon of the 25th at check-point 2, and he had told me that there was a Serb military doctor who was involved in looking at the condition of wounded and that they had been involved in that process.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is when the wounded were in question. But did he tell you that anyone hindered the evacuation of the civilian population and whether -- of the Palic or UNHCR or UNPROFOR representatives requested that the rest be evacuated as well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Tolimir repeat the entire question. The interpreter simply did not understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the interpreters asked you to repeat the question because they are not sure if they understood it correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Based on what you could see in the reports of UNHCR and UNPROFOR representatives as well as civilian affairs representatives, could you conclude that the evacuation of civilians from Zepa was carried out without any hindrance by the VRS, as Mr. Joseph wrote in his report and as he testified here before you?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I reflected yesterday in my testimony on the atmosphere amongst the civilian population, as described to me by Captain Tom Dibb, being very tense in the Zepa enclave and that whenever there were Bosnian Serb, you know, military people around, you know, the tension levels were very high. So that's really all I can speak to on -- on that front. The people I met from the Zepa War Presidency, I think I've also reflected that the impression that I formed very strongly was that they were frightened and under duress. So I can't really speak to anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at reports of some other people involved in the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P585. It is Louis Fortin's diary. Page 143, please, in the Serbian, and 140 in the English. It is the entry for the 21st of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This should not be broadcast because it's confidential.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, I wonder if I may have some more water. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. The Court Usher will assist you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have it in the English language but not in Serbian still. Page 143 in the Serbian please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It reads as follows: "A meeting between General Gobillard General Harland on the 21st of July' --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please give a reference from which part you are reading.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We can see on the screen that it concerns the 1st of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P585, page 143 in the Serbian, and page 140 in the English. The entry for the 21st of July, 1995, and not for the 1st of May, 1995. 21st of July, 1995. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, we don't have it in English yet. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention it's still the wrong page. The page number is correct as quoted by General Tolimir. Page 140 does reflect the meeting on 21st of July. So I'm not sure. Maybe there's a different version in e-court. There we go. Got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. This is page 143 in B/C/S and 140 in the English. Please go ahead, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank Mr. Thayer. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we should consider if it's appropriate to read this text into the transcript because it's a confidential document. But I'm not quite sure if that is really the fact because we saw some pages with redactions. Can you tell us, or perhaps Mr. Thayer, if we have the redacted version of the confidential version on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, there are two levels of redactions going on. One is that -- which were imposed upon the OTP by the provider. The second -- and that is placing it under seal and referring to the contents in private session. So, Mr. President, you are correct. I was actually discussing with Ms. Stewart whether to stand up, given the content. The redactions that we see, to which Your Honour is referring, the blacking out, refers to very, very personal, purely personal matters which Colonel Fortin had wished to be redacted. This, again, was a personal diary of his. I think you heard about this when he testified. So that's what the actual blacked out parts refer to. That's independent of the Rule 70 restrictions that were placed upon us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps you can help us if there is any problem with reading out some portions of this diary into the record, or should that be in private session and the public part be redacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think it really should be in private session, Mr. President, to comply with the Rule 70 restrictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In that case, we should turn into private session. And the parts you have read out, Mr. Tolimir, should be redacted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. By my mistake, we left the courtroom for our first break in private session. We are now back in open session. Before Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination, I would like to ask Mr. Gajic to clarify one thing. We heard your submission, your response, to a motion of the Prosecution to convert some witnesses from viva voce to 98 bis respectively, 92 ter. Your response was only related to one witness, you discussed yesterday, and not the others. Does that mean that you will respond to the motion of the Prosecution in writing? Just to clarify the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, of course, my response had to do with one witness only. We will submit the remainder of our response in writing. We will do so because that is what the Court Officer asked to us do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is clear now. Mr. Tolimir, you may continue your cross-examination. Will you still deal with the last document we had -- or still have on the screen? In that case, we should go into private session. Otherwise, you may continue in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I will not be using the document anymore. I will be asking the witness about her knowledge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Sayer, a moment ago we discussed a document which contained a public statement made by Silajdzic to the general public and UNPROFOR. Therefore, it was in the public domain. Do you remember, we just discussed it, if General Smith --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you see Mr. Thayer on his feet. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I'm going to keep getting on my feet if General Tolimir is going to build into his questions statements that are just unsupported by the record. If he would just the question without building in these misstatements. I don't think there's anything in that portion that suggests that it was a public record, that it was a public statement. To the contrary. It was a meeting between General Gobillard and Mr. Silajdzic. So I'm going to keep standing up as long as he keeps misrepresenting the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think Mr. Thayer is correct. We saw a record -- a reference to a specific meeting which was not a public meeting. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wasn't referring to the meeting. I was referring to Mr. Silajdzic's statement for the press and UNPROFOR, which is clearly referenced here. If Mr. Thayer wants to keep this confidential, he may do so, but I do believe that the public is already aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... No, this is not the problem. You said, We saw a document about a public statement made by Silajdzic. The document was not related to a public statement. Perhaps there was a public statement, but the document was not referring to that. Please choose your words very carefully. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Did you hear a public broadcast of a statement where Mr. Silajdzic stated that he wanted to assist the evacuation of civilians from Zepa but that he also wanted them to stay there in order for the Serbs to have blood on their hands once they capture Zepa? Is this something you heard broadcast? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't recall hearing a broadcast, a public broadcast, in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you were present at meetings where you were able to hear things and you read reports, this is my question for you: Did General Smith, through his action or inaction in stalling the negotiations surrounding the all-for-all exchange, contribute to the wish of Silajdzic to have the Muslims remain in Zepa in order for the Serbs to be compelled to seize it and to get blood on their hands? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any action that General Smith took in order to stall the negotiations surrounding an all-for-all prisoner exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show D56 now, please. Or D55. Whichever is easier for e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document to appear, I'll put my question to you. We'll have a look at what General Smith was doing. We see the fall of Zepa there. This is a document produced by Bezruchenko. You must have met him in your time there. He was at the UNPROFOR HQ and appeared as an expert for the Prosecution here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not an appropriate way to ask for a document. This or that. You should decide which document you want to have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I want this document, page 30. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which one is it? D56 or D55?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D55. Page 30, paragraph 108. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm quoting from paragraph 108. You have it there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown the paragraph which is at the bottom in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is what Mr. Bezruchenko had to say as an expert for the Prosecution: "Following the meeting between General Smith and Hamdija Torlak on 126th of July, 285th brigade commander Avdo Palic sent a dramatic appeal for help to BIH President Alija Izetbegovic and General Staff commander Rasim Delic." What follows below is the entire telegram which I'm not going to quote in its entirety but only one portion. It reads: "President, at about 2100 hours, negotiations in Boksanica ... were concluded at which General Smith; Torlak, Hamdija, president of the executive board of Zepa, and war criminal Ratko Mladic were present." I would like to skip the next four or lines to quote from line 6: "During the negotiations, General Smith stated that our side did not accept the agreement about the exchange of all for all and that our side was looking for some additional concessions. Hamdija Torlak remained at the place of negotiations in Boksanica and he was told that if we were ready for an all-for-all exchange, during the night or until 0800 hours in the morning, General Smith will let us know, so that a plan of helicopter evacuation could be prepared." What is the extent of your knowledge about this, since on the 26th, as you say, you were present at a meeting with Hamdija Torlak, General Mladic, and General Smith? You were able to see an image of that.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that there was a discussion between -- well, General Smith reflected the comments that President Izetbegovic and Minister Muratovic and Minister Masovic had made the evening before, and there was definitely conversation, I can recall, about a helicopter evacuation being supported by UNPROFOR. But I don't believe that the Bosnian Serb side agreed to the helicopter evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Emma. My question didn't have to do with helicopters. Can you tell me whether mention was made at the meeting and whether General Smith said that the Bosnian side was not agreeing to the all-for-all exchange and that it was asking for additional concessions? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't recall that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have line 11 of the same text now, where it reads: "We cannot believe that this problem looks like you will not solve it. If this problem is not resolved in the course of tomorrow, we [sic] must make a decision tomorrow to make a breakthrough in your direction with 2.000 men and 10.000 rounds ... whoever will cross over, and you have the picture of Srebrenica," and so on. This is my question: In this telegram that Avdo Palic sent to Izetbegovic, did he express his protest about the fact that the army was being compelled to break through out of the encirclement?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am reading this document in front of me for the first time. And I should probably let you know that I never personally met Avdo Palic, so I cannot speak to whether this is an accurate reflection of what he said or not. I have no knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Sayer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at line 16 now of the same telegram sent by Avdo Palic to Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It reads: "I am appealing to you on behalf of combatants or fighters who have for the past 15 days been fighting like lions. I ask you in the name of fallen soldiers. And in my ranks have I sons or parents of those who died. I ask you in the name of the evacuated families and children who are -- who can't wait to meet with their fathers who are left on the Zepa mountain to be slaughtered or annihilated in any other way. I ask you again in the name of my soldiers to make it possible for us to defend Bosnia in some other battle-fields." Since you were saying yesterday that General Smith was not aware of Avdo Palic's position, did he express his position in public to his Presidency in the telegrams, and did he not in this document publicly say that he supported Torlak as his representative who was waiting at Boksanica for a response? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refer to my earlier answer, that I've never seen this document before or met Mr. Palic. So General Smith -- the only conversation that I am aware that General Smith had about Avdo Palic was when Minister Muratovic was pressing him very hard to state whether Avdo Palic had signed the agreement of the 24th of July that had been signed by the Zepa War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, how can I understand your last question? You said: "Did he express his position in public to his president in the telegrams?" What do you mean by the words "in public"? Is your understanding that a telegram to a president is a public statement?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President, for allowing me to state my mind. I should have said "clearly," "jasno," rather than "publicly," "javno." Maybe I misspoke. What I meant was, did he not state it clearly to Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This clarifies the situation. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Can we go back to page 23 of this report now. This is Bezruchenko's report about the fall of Zepa. Let's look at paragraph 86 on page 23. Thank you. We see it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Bezruchenko says: "UNPROFOR, Sector Sarajevo, at this point UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo began preparations for evacuations of civilians from Zepa. UNPROFOR operations order dated 20 July made the following assessment of the situation." And I'm quoting the translation from English. "BiH defence of Zepa has collapsed, and surrender of the enclave to VRS has been accepted. Large numbers of displaced persons wishing to seek refuge in the Federation-controlled territory will therefore have to moved." And in footnote 131 you can see the original title of the document in English. Have you read it? Do you remember? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my role at headquarters UNPROFOR, I did not read OP orders from Sector Sarajevo which was commanded by General Gobillard. They would normally have been dealt with either by the Chief of Staff, General Nicolai, or -- or by Colonel Baxter. So I haven't seen this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's look at paragraph 87 now. The order determined the UNPROFOR mission as follows; I'm quoting from the English translation: "In conjunction with BiH government and UNHCR, UNPROFOR is to coordinate the evacuation of displaced persons from Zepa to Zenica." And in footnote 132, we have the referenced document, which you would have to read for yourself in English. I don't read English. This is my question. In these operational orders issued by UNPROFOR that I've just quoted from, is there a position expressed that UNPROFOR should get involved in the evacuation of the population or, rather, of the displaced persons from Zepa to Zenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The text says that UNPROFOR is to coordinate the evacuation of DPs from Zepa to Zenica, which is rather different than to organise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for stating with precision what was written there. That's true; UNPROFOR was supposed to coordinate. Thank you. If you can, look at paragraph 88, which states as follows: "The evacuation operation was supposed to be executed in three stages and involve UNPROFOR forces of Sector Sarajevo, Sector North-East, Sector South-West, as well as HQ UNPROFOR." And he explained it in footnote 133. He said that these were the organisations that UNPROFOR was supposed to coordinate. Is that what you had in mind when you specified that it had to do with coordination between UNPROFOR? Was it these other organisations that were supposed to be involved in that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should clarify. I haven't seen any of the specific OP orders that are referenced in the footnotes to this document. But normally a military OP order would, you know, include a great deal more detail than the very small extracts that have been highlighted in this report that you've just read at paras 88 and -- yeah, at paragraph 88.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you didn't read or see them, does it mean that there were no documents produced on the 20th of July as operational orders of the Sector Sarajevo HQ? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, what is that kind of question? She -- the witness clearly stated that she hasn't read it. You -- you can't draw from that that there were no documents like that. This is not helping.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I put my question, and she can say, I know, I don't know, whether the question is stupid, logical, or illogical. I merely put it as it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then my answer would be that the question is illogical as -- merely the fact that I haven't --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- read it doesn't mean that they don't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is my next question: Were you actively involved in the developments surrounding Zepa? Can you tell us when it was that UNPROFOR commenced engaging in preparations for the evacuation of the civilians from Zepa, and what did it -- the preparations involve? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I can clarify, as I testified yesterday, that my primary role within headquarters UNPROFOR working for General Smith was as the liaison officer with the Bosnian Presidency and the Croat -- and the Federation. It was unusual for me to be involved in Bosnian Serb-held territory, and the only reason that I was involved in the meetings that was discussed at length yesterday was because my colleague Captain Tom Dibb was already deployed in the Zepa enclave. My role is -- was largely on these visits to keep notes, to act as an interpreter when required, and to, you know, observe as -- as part of General Smith's party, what was going on, on the ground. I hope that helps explain that I did not have a role in the strategy or the operational control of UNPROFOR's operations at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, my question is this: Did General Smith and his party, together with you, do anything to allow or to create the conditions which would allow the civilian population to remain in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the documents that we saw yesterday made reference to UNPROFOR's mandate, and General Smith was very clear throughout the time he was on the ground at check-point 2 what UNPROFOR could do and what we couldn't do. Specifically we were not able to guarantee any part of the agreement that was signed, for example, on the 24th of July by the Zepa War Presidency. So I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do the provisions of that agreement provide any security guarantees to the departing population in keeping with the agreement itself, any guarantees during the period of the war? And we refer to paragraph 7, I believe.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 7, I believe, as we saw yesterday, did reference the Geneva Convention. The point that I'm making is that General Smith, my -- I have a very clear recollection that General Smith was extremely clear with both General Mladic and the members of the War Presidency that UNPROFOR could not sign or be party as a guarantor to that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for stressing that. Does it mean that under the agreement provisions the population of Zepa was supposed to be evacuated and eventually allowed to return once the war was over? Were they allowed to do that? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we spoke yesterday about the phrase "to freely choose." The population were supposed to have the ability to freely choose where they wanted to live. And as I reflected yesterday, from my conversations with Captain Dibb, the impression that was formed by him and passed to me was that the local population did not feel that they had freedom to choose. They were leaving because they were afraid and they felt there were no other options. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us this, please: Does Dudnik's signature, who was UNPROFOR representative and UNPROFOR commander in Zepa, provides any legitimacy to him to sign that agreement? Was it his -- done on his personal own behalf, or did he do that on behalf of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak to what was in Colonel Dudnik's mind when he signed the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether it was the position of General Smith in his conversations with General Mladic and Torlak was his own personal position, or did he act on behalf of UNPROFOR HQ? Who did he act on -- on whose behalf did he act?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, really, that's a question for General Smith. But General Smith was commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: What about Colonel Dudnik? Was he not the commander of UNPROFOR in the enclave of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the colonel of the Ukrainian contingent of UNPROFOR in the enclave of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the UNPROFOR contingent under the command of Sector Sarajevo and the UN forces in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at some footage concerning Zepa to see what the representatives at the negotiations had to do about the security of the population. It is P740. You can see some people in this still whom you had recognised as being Mr. Torlak and General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you now play the footage, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you able to hear what General Mladic said or perhaps to read the subtitles? What did he tell Mr. Torlak about the able-bodied men as part of the column that was passing through the Boksanica check-point? Didn't he tell him that there were some able-bodied men there?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subtitles indicated that he did refer to able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you hear Mr. Torlak's answer? What did he tell the General?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sorry, I -- I heard the bit about the coffee and the sugar. But I'm not sure about his answer to the last bit. Perhaps if it could be replayed, if that's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It is, since they were not taken out of the convoy but were actually allowed to proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Were you able to read Mr. Hamdija's response whereby he said that there weren't that many?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did read that in the subtitles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you hear General Mladic say, I don't want to see any more of them coming in?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's up on the screen in front of me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it mean that they were actually allowed to proceed? And they were able-bodied men, as both Mladic and Torlak agreed. Because Torlak said that there weren't that many.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have -- I have no knowledge of this exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. You could hear it, and you also saw Mr. Joseph's report, where he says that he managed to evacuate everyone from the list successfully. Does it mean that the VRS did not at all check the age in order to ascertain who -- which men were of military age and which were not during the evacuation of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next see Exhibit P585 again. It is Fortin's diary. Could we have page 56, the entry for the 25th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should not be broadcast. And if you want to read anything from that document, we have to go into private session, I'm afraid. But this ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wanted to read out certain portions. Because Mr. Fortin did not want to have that under seal. We made use of this in public session when he testified. In any case, I will abide by your instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Thayer can help us, if there is a need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, as of yet, I don't know exactly what portion we're talking about. So I'm afraid I can't help the Court right now. In a moment I may be able to, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The same portion was read out during Mr. Fortin's testimony. I will read it out. If Mr. Thayer believes that it should not be made public, I will not object. However, it was red out in public once before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be very helpful if you could give us the relevant part, indicate the page number, to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In this section of Colonel Fortin's diary, there are a number of entries for various meetings and conversations throughout the day on the 25th. So if we could have page numbers, as Your Honour asked for, and a time, because he identifies a lot of these meetings by time, that would be particularly helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It is P585. P585. It is already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This is on the screen. We were asking for a page number and a date of the entry you want to read out.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Page 156. The entry for the 25th of July, 1995, concerning the enclave of Zepa. It is about a meeting between General Janvier, Smith, and Gobillard. The last paragraph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page is it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, I -- the reason I asked for the time is that there are a number of meetings. If we're referring to the meeting that begins at 0930 hours, that begins on page 155 in the English, not 156, if the General is interested in the witness being able to read the actual account of the meeting from the beginning. It begins on 155. It's a meeting at the airport, 25 July, 0930 hours. I don't know if that's what General Tolimir is referring to, but that's where it begins in English, page 155.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't know if that is the page we have on the screen at the moment. There is mentioning of a meeting between Generals Janvier, Smith, and Gobillard at the airport, 25th of July, 0930 hours. But I don't see that -- oh, yes, it's also on the B/C/S on the left side of the screen. Is there any problem to deal with that in a public session, Mr. Thayer?
