utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think to stay on the right side of the Rule 70 restrictions that have been imposed we should remain in private session whether or not it came in, in public inadvertently through Colonel Fortin. I think, as the Trial Chamber's already noted, that is the requirement for this document from the Rule 70 provider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. We will turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could we please have P1980. We saw that document yesterday. It is the Baxter report. The witness provided some answers regarding it in view of some Prosecution questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you this: Do you recall whether Mr. Louis Fortin attended the meeting as well? The meeting was held on the 28th of July, 1995. Sorry, the 27th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which meeting are you referring to, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The meeting between Smith and Mladic that Mr. Baxter refers to in his report. It was on the 27th, and I believe the report was drafted on the 28th. It was discussed yesterday during our hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where in this document - page 1 we have on the screen - can we find a reference to that meeting? It would help the Chamber and witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Paragraph 4. Could we also have that paragraph in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Was the meeting attended by Mr. Fortin, who actually referred to the meeting here? Apologies, no, this is the Baxter report. And we will see Fortin's report about the same topic a bit later.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't recall Mr. Fortin being at the meeting. There were a number of Sector Sarajevo staff in the -- the Zepa enclave. It's possible that he had travelled in one of their vehicles, but he certainty had not been part of General Smith's party, in the vehicles that -- that we travelled to check-point 2 in.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at para 4: "General Smith explains to Mladic that the Bosnian government were unlikely to accept this agreement as they had had no direct involvement," as you yourself stated during your testimony. I continue: "... and they ultimately held the POWs who were being offered for exchange. Mladic scornfully replied that Muratovic had had ample opportunity to meet with Mladic at OP-2 but had consistently refused the offer. Mladic asked General Smith to inform the Bosnian government that the agreement had been signed, and those men in Zepa who refused to surrender their weapons by 1800 hours would be liquidated."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see what else Baxter has to say -- sorry, Fortin, at page 585.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... again, very confusing. You should put a question to the witness. You have read out into the record a certain part of this document. You should put a question to the witness before you move to another part of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you discuss the word "liquidation" yesterday as something that General Mladic told General Smith, which astounded you, as you said?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't the word "liquidation" that astounded me yesterday. But yesterday we did talk about my recollection specifically of this phrase that they would be liquidated if they refused to surrender their weapons by the deadline of 1800 hours; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this standard military lingo, a military term that would be used in order to treat an enemy who is refusing to lay down weapons, especially if it is all taking place within a demilitarised zone?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it's standard military terminology to talk about liquidating people of the opposing side, no. Certainly not in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how the British Army interprets what needs to be done with the enemy if they continue providing resistance in a territory already under the control of the British Army? Let's use the example of the Falkland Islands, for example.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if there is a battle going on, as there was in the Falkland Islands, between two parties, it continues until there is either a surrender or some form of peace accord. So the fighting would continue --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember how many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the witness has not finished the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. But, you know, in -- using the Falklands as an example, I do not believe that, in any of the books I have read about the Falklands from the Generals who were responsible for that campaign, the term, you know "liquidating the enemy" was not used. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the English army invade the Falkland Islands and their population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we are not dealing with the Falkland war in this courtroom. The witness is not called as a witness in this trial to testify about the Falkland conflict. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The witnesses herself said that in Britain weapons were not used to prevent such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you tell us, did you have any knowledge about there being fighting going on between the Serbs and Muslims in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is a misstatement. The witness didn't say that. Put a question to the witness in relation to the facts, to Zepa, and the involvement of this witness in the negotiations and the UNPROFOR activities. Carry on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Sayer, tell us, were the Muslims in Zepa armed, and did they mount resistance to the Army of Republika Srpska? And was it for this reason that negotiations were taking place for their surrender of weapons and for the agreement that -- that was ultimately signed? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there was a -- an armed force of Armija BH soldiers within the Zepa enclave. Indeed, we've spoken about their commander, Avdo Palic. But, as we mentioned, has already been mentioned, part of the discussion between Minister Muratovic and General Smith focussed on whether Avdo Palic had been party to the agreement that had been signed by the Zepa War Presidency, because the -- Minister Muratovic felt that Mr. Palic had not, that this had not been signed with the agreement of the Armija troops on the ground in Zepa. I hope that clarifies my answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, following the talks between General Smith and Muratovic, did Muratovic realize that the army in Zepa agreed to lay down their weapons and not to take part in any further combat? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall General Smith explaining to Minister Muratovic that he had not met Mr. Palic during his visits to OP-2 in Zepa. So they would not have had that exchange that formed the part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did representatives of UNPROFOR talk to and were they in contact with Avdo Palic? And did Avdo Palic pass through Boksanica as each and every bus carrying inhabitants of Zepa traversed the area? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that he passed through the check-point 2 at any time. I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now show P585, please. Page 136 in Serbian and 156 in English. This is Fortin's diary which speaks to the same event --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I've just stopped you because we have to go into private session first. Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is my question: Were you present during the part of the negotiations when General Mladic told General Smith that Muslim soldiers should turn over their weapons or else fighting will continue and they would be killed if they hold on to their weapon? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: As a soldier, you were a soldier at the time, do you believe it legitimate for a commander to decide to continue engaging in combat against those who refused to sign agreement on cessation of combat? Is that a legitimate decision, in your view?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, if you were in a combat situation and the fighting is continuing and you end up having a situation where you are able to take prisoners of the opposing side, there should be no question that prisoners would be liquidated simply because they had refused to surrender their weapons. Once you've taken them prisoner, you have to abide by the Geneva Convention on the rule regarding prisoners. So it's perfectly acceptable to remove their weapons from them and hold them as prisoners. It is not, in my belief, acceptable to kill them once you've taken them as prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did General Mladic refer to taking these soldiers prisoner or about continuing with the fighting unless they agreed to surrender their weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refer back to the note that I largely authored about this exchange, where Mladic gave an ultimatum that if the men of fighting age refused to surrender their weapons by the deadline he set of 1800 hours, that they would be liquidated. I -- I wrote -- my notes accurately reflected what General Mladic said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell us, did the Muslims refuse to surrender weapons up until the deadline indicated in the agreement and in General Mladic's statement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- we weren't in the enclave at the time of the -- the deadline, so I -- I believe that there were men of fighting age that refused to surrender, but I didn't personally see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you come to learn from anyone, either from UNPROFOR or from any of the warring parties during the negotiations and your three-day stay in Zepa, that the Muslim army did not wish to surrender weapons and to surrender at the UN base, as indicated in the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think I've reflected in my testimony already, I did -- my impression from speaking to Captain Dibb and others was that the members, the men of fighting age within the enclave who were part of the Armija force, had little confidence in their being treated properly as prisoners of war if they surrendered their weapons. And certainly that was a fear that was also relayed at the meeting that happened in the early hours of the morning at the Presidency on the 25th/26th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you testifying here about what it was that soldiers whom you didn't see were thinking or about what General Mladic said to General Smith about the agreement and adherence to it or violation of it by one of the two sides? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, your question put to the witness was: "Did you come to learn from anyone, either from UNPROFOR or from any of the warring parties during the negotiations," and so on. You were asking for that. So that I'm surprised by the way you put the next question to the witness. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm asking her, in the question that surprises you, whether she's testifying about the views held by the soldiers who refused to surrender weapons or about the events that happened in the relevant time-period. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I -- my answer relayed the impression gained from Captain Dibb who was within the Zepa town throughout that period, and also, you know, the questions that were asked by members of the Bosnian Presidency in the meeting between General Smith, President Izetbegovic, and Ministers Muratovic and Masovic on the late evening of the 25th of July and early hours of the morning of the 26th of July, when, you know, President Izetbegovic and Minister Muratovic both expressed their fear that even if they agreed to an all-for-all prisoner exchange, that the fighters, the Bosnian fighters within the Zepa enclave, would -- would still be subject to atrocities by the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was their fear justified and was it materialised, in reality?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, their fear was justifiably based on the experience that had just occurred in Srebrenica, which, in conversations between General Mladic and General Smith, General Mladic had claimed had been finished in the correct way, and yet, in this particular period, there was a growing amount of information and evidence that suggested very significant numbers of people, of men, had been killed, as they -- as they sought a way to Federation territory from the enclave of Srebrenica. So, in my opinion, I could understand why President Izetbegovic and Minister Muratovic were afraid that the situation in Zepa would deteriorate along the same lines, and this is why I believe they were very keen to have any weapons that would be surrendered, surrendered to UNPROFOR and not to BSA, and Minister Muratovic was desperate for the evacuation to take place by helicopter rather than by road.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you spoke of the agreement by the War Presidency on the surrender of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have P736 shown. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It was signed by the three-member Presidency, as discussed in your cross-examination yesterday. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall us speaking about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you remember this, do you see here a document which the War Presidency of Zepa issued and signed? It was signed by the three representatives of the War Presidency of the municipality of Zepa: Mehmed Hajric, Hamdija Torlak, and Amir Imamovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the body of the text of this decision in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We'll be reading the first paragraph of the decision, below the headline decision. "All the able-bodied men aged 18 to 55 shall surrender their weapons to representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska in the presence of UNPROFOR at the UNPROFOR base in Zepa. All the able-bodied men shall be registered by the ICRC and shall be guarded by the forces of the VRS in the presence of UNPROFOR in Zepa until an agreement on the exchange has been reached. "All the able-bodied men registered by the ICRC shall, once the agreement is reached on the exchange and the exchange of prisoners of war, be safely escorted by UNPROFOR and evacuated to the territory of their choosing. Urgently inform the Muslim authorities in Sarajevo of this decision and carry it out forthwith. 27th of July, 1995," signed by the three members who took the decision, as well as by Rajko Kusic and General Mladic, who kept this as a guarantee that weapons would be surrendered. This is my question: In keeping with the decision of the War Presidency, did the Muslims surrender their weapons to the VRS and UNPROFOR, and did they ultimately came to the UNPROFOR base? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I -- I don't know the full answer to that question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And did Muslim soldiers come to the UNPROFOR base to surrender their weapons, as this decision indicates? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I can't speak to that, as I was never at the UNPROFOR base in the centre of Zepa town. That's where my colleague Captain Tom Dibb was.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you testified to this document, and it was admitted through you. Is there anything you can tell us about this document that you have knowledge of?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can testify again that when General Smith spoke to the three members of the War Presidency that had signed this document, and General Mladic, he explained that he felt it was unlikely that the Bosnian government would accept the agreement, and I -- I did -- there is a part in the meeting note. There is a couple of paragraphs specifically about that that we did read yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, did you and General Smith know which were the provisions because of which the Bosnian government refused to accept this agreement, or was behind it the intention harboured by Silajdzic to have the Serbian army capture Zepa and bloody their hands? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you what General Smith said at the time and is noted in the meeting note was that the -- he felt the Bosnian government were unlikely to accept the agreement because they had not been party to it. And there had been a long exchange between -- of messages that we had conveyed from the Bosnian Presidency to General Mladic, trying to find an agreement between the two sides, for Minister Muratovic to meet with General Mladic. And as I said yesterday, General Mladic refused to go to the airport and Minister Muratovic refused to come to check-point 2. And so General Smith reiterated the fact that he felt it was unlikely that the Bosnian government would accept it, as they had not been party to drawing it up. I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if the Muslim army was aware that a meeting had to take place between Mladic and Muratovic, and was it -- was that the reason why they did not surrender their weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you know who gave up on signing the agreement? Was it the Army of Republika Srpska or the Muslim side for whom this decision was intended, to begin with? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify which agreement you're referring to? Are you referring to the prisoner of war exchange or this particular agreement that we have in front of us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I mean the agreement we have in front of us. We read a moment ago Palic's statement that General Smith had said that the Muslim government was placing additional conditions on the signing of the agreement.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that the statement that we saw from Mr. Palic was that General Smith had reflected they were placing additional conditions on the prisoner of war exchange rather than this agreement. But perhaps I misunderstood you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. My question was this: Did the Army of Republika Srpska give up on this decision, or was it the Muslim army, members of whom should have surrendered their weapons and who were the subject of this decision? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was that General Mladic's patience had run out and that is why he gave the ultimatum of, you know, the deadline of 1800 hours for the total surrender of the Armija forces within the Zepa enclave. He certainly, in that exchange that we saw in the meeting note, was adamant that he would not meet, you know, Muratovic at the airport and said that Muratovic had had plenty of opportunity to come to check-point 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it's time for our second break. We must have our break now, and we'll resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I would like to raise, briefly, a minor matter. I've heard from -- that the Prosecution would like to change the surrogate sheet for the Exhibit P594 because it incorrectly refers to P1756. If that is correct and my understanding is correct, then this will be granted.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may do that. We should continue. And I would like to ask, Mr. Tolimir, can you give us an estimation of the length of the remainder of the cross-examination? Is that possible?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think we'll take another 15 minutes, depending on the answers I receive. The rest is beyond my ability to assess. Much will depend on the answers I receive from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That's absolutely fine. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Ms. Sayer, you wanted to see what Mr. Palic had to say about what Smith told Torlak at the meeting. Perhaps I can give it to you, if you still insist on seeing that. Otherwise, I'll move on. It is a single sentence which I can quote.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D55. Page 30, paragraph 108. It is Mr. Bezruchenko's report which he drafted as an OTP expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see page 29 in the English and page 30 in the Serbian. Let us again look at line 6, in the third paragraph, where we see the text in small font. It says: "During the negotiations, General Smith stated that our side deadlined to accept the agreement on the exchange all for all and that we were asking for additional concessions." Next, he also says that we cannot believe that you seem unwilling to resolve this issue. Then in line 16, it says: "I am asking you on behalf of the fighters who have been fighting during the last 15 days," and so on. Perhaps now can you tell us what you wanted to say about whether, in this telegram by Avdo Palic sent to Alija Izetbegovic, Palic said that he - that is to say Izetbegovic - was unwilling to resolve the exchange all for all and was this conveyed to the Muslim side, since you were present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting I was present at late in the evening of the 25th/early hours of the 26th of July between General Smith and President Izetbegovic, at that meeting, President Izetbegovic had stated that he was very open to pursuing an all-for-all prisoner exchange but that they were -- the Bosnian side was concerned that the BSA would not uphold their side of the agreement. I -- at that meeting in the late hours of -- of 25th/early hours of the 26th, there was no mention of concessions -- sorry, of additional concessions being required by the Bosnian Presidency side that this document on the screen in front of us refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us look at line 8 where it's -- Avdo Palic says: "During the night, or that is to say in the morning before 8.00, General Smith needs to be informed so that a plan could be drawn for the helicopter evacuation." Can we see that in the telegram by Avdo Palic whereby he refers to the meeting of 8.00 which you have just described?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A part of that sentence we can see in the English version in line 1 and the following lines.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see -- I can see the lines on the screen in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is this: Was UNPROFOR making any plans for helicopter evacuation, such as referred to by Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The question of helicopter evacuation did -- was raised by Minister Muratovic at that meeting, and General Smith -- I recall General Smith discussing it, and I believe he stated his view, that he thought that it was unlikely that General Mladic would allow a helicopter evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And we saw that in the agreement General Mladic was willing to release them. So was it all left to whether Smith and Muratovic could be believed or not, or were there any other positions involved?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that the agreement makes any mention of General Mladic agreeing to release the men of fighting age by helicopter evacuation. So I'm not sure what -- what your question refers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Having quoted this document, we are now going back again to the War Presidency decision to see what it says there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, in the meantime, could we go on to page 31 in the Serbian of this document. We can stay on this page in the English. I'm interested in paragraph 109.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Alija Izetbegovic says as follows, on the 26th of July, 1995. I'm quoting paragraph 109, the small print: "There is information that a certain number of your soldiers is moving towards the village with an intention to surrender. I do not know if it is correct. Warn them about the danger and put them under control. Negotiations about an exchange are in progress. We have sufficient arguments to obtain good conditions for the exchange because we keep a great number of their prisoners. However, we have to be careful about what we are doing. Something else, by the way, it is important to burn the entire archive and letters."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go to page 110 -- actually, paragraph 110, which spills over to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let's look at this portion that we can see and then we'll move on to the next. On the 26th of July, 1995, at 700 hours, Colonel Palic sent his last desperate message to President Izetbegovic. This time Palic was direct to the point of being impolite. I quote: "Mr. President," you can see the two first lines in English, "we received both your letters and the agreement you sent to us. I ask you, and let this remind -- remain only for you and me, are you ready to exchange us, the people of Zepa, which number about two and a half thousand with the people who arrived from Srebrenica, for all the Chetniks? We emphasise that half of the people have no weapons, and we have no chances of breaking through. Reply to us until 8.00 in the morning so we know how to behave, because our representative Hamdija Torlak and criminal Mladic are still at Boksanica. And one more question, are you ready to pay for the expenses of our evacuation by helicopter if UNPROFOR accepted it?" My question is this: Well, it also says, in paragraph 110, Mr. Bezruchenko states that this message did not end with the traditional greeting of "Salaam" and that therefore he deemed it as a last desperate attempt. Was Palic stalling any surrender so that the civilians be allowed to leave Zepa and so that what Silajdzic had said would come true, meaning that the Serbs would have blood on their hands by having been forced to take Zepa by force?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my impression from the document. My impression from the document is that he was requesting information from the president of the Bosnian government as to what action he should take as the head of the Armija forces within the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In this telegram is he reporting to Alija that the official representative of Zepa, Mr. Torlak, was at Boksanica?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the English translation from the previous page did -- did say, yes. No, on this page, sorry, on page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I promised to show you again P736, in paragraph 2 of the decision. I will make good on this promise, and afterwards I will conclude my cross-examination. We can see again the Presidency decision, the third paragraph, which reads: All able-bodied men ... registered by the ICRC ... shall, following the signing of an agreement on the exchange of POWs, be -- will be safe and escorted by UNPROFOR. They will be evacuated to a location of their own choosing. Can you see General Mladic's signature on the document at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see it in the Serbian version, but -- yes, now. Now I can see the translation on the right-hand side of the screen. And can I clarify, this is actually the War Presidency, the Zepa War Presidency, decision, rather than the Bosnian Presidency. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever act as a military analyst during your career?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you did, is it your conclusion, then, that it was Palic who was asking the Presidency whether they were ready to accept something? Was it your conclusion whether the commander of the army in Zepa, Mr. Palic, was actually being suspicious of the intentions of his Presidency on the evacuation of the soldiers from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, my conclusion is somewhat different. My conclusion from the document that we've seen, from the telegram from Mr. Palic to President Izetbegovic, is that it has a note of desperation in the form of language that is used. And that is perhaps indicative of Palic's recognition that the time is continuing to pass rather rapidly towards the ultimatum that General Mladic has given the Bosnian Muslim men of fighting age whom Palic commands. So that would be my conclusion, that this is a request from the military, the Bosnian military commander on the ground, for clarity from his political commander, his president, as to what course of action he should take.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was Palic's request in accordance with the military situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't understand your question. I think it -- Palic's request seems to emanate from the military situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you for this answer. Thank you for all the answers you provided during your testimony. I thank you for coming here. On behalf of this Defence and my own, we wish you a safe journey home. May God bless you. We have no further questions of you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this concludes our examination of the witness. I'd like to thank to all those who had sufficient patience to bear with us, since I believe we made a number of mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your words, Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Thayer, do you have re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. President. I should -- I will conclude before the end of today. If we could have that document back up, just very quickly. That was P736. I just want to pick up where General Tolimir left off.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, ma'am, good afternoon to you.

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: General Tolimir read you to the paragraph that's just above Roman numeral II in both versions. He referred to the portion where this document states that the POWs would be escorted by UNPROFOR. I want to just focus your attention for a second on the paragraph that's right above that one, where this document says that: "All able-bodied men shall be registered by the ICRC and shall be guarded by the forces of the VRS in the presence of UNPROFOR in Zepa ..." My question to you is: Based on your experience on the ground, participating in the various meetings, discussions, how did the Muslims in Zepa feel about ever being guarded by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression is that the Bosnian Muslim population in the Zepa enclave were extremely nervous about the proposal of being guarded by the Bosnian Serb army at any time. And that as the time passed, over the three days, the request for UNPROFOR to take a more active role than observing became more regular.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: War is a nerve-wracking experience and people are often nervous in war. Was there anything that you were aware of in terms of the Muslim population that was communicated to you that suggested to you why they were nervous about ever being guarded by the VRS?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I met with Captain Tom Dibb, he did reflect that some of the people that he had spoken to in Zepa town had spoken to people who had arrived in the town in the wake of the Srebrenica events. And as a result, you know, rumours of what had happened at Srebrenica had spread amongst the civilian population in Zepa quite rapidly, and for this reason they -- there were -- they were very afraid of being left in the power of the Bosnian Serb army, whether they were women or men of fighting age.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, at page 8 of today's transcript, line 22, you stated that -- and I'll just quote exactly what you said. You said: "They were repeatedly -- Mr. Torlak asked for the use of helicopters, because they did not believe that road transport would be safe." The -- I just want to ask you what you understood from your discussions and attending these meetings this reference to, as you put it, "the road transport would not be safe" referred to? Are they afraid of driving off a cliff, are they afraid of pot holes? What about the road transport was it that they were afraid about?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. To clarify, they were afraid that the -- that the buses would not be allowed through to the Bosnian-held territory without interference from the Bosnian Serb forces. Specifically they were afraid that there would be segregation of men of fighting age and also perhaps women of a certain age, as had happened in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I think just before the last break we took there were some questions put to you about the term, the meaning of the term "liquidate" and your testimony about General Mladic using that term. Do you remember what you said in your OTP witness statement exactly about the impression that you drew from this particular encounter with General Mladic when he made this statement?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do recall in my witness statement reflecting my impression that General Mladic's demeanour had hardened over the course of the three days, and I specifically noted the use of the phrase "liquidated" to make sure it went into our record of the day, day's events.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall exactly what you said with respect to whether liquidation would apply to armed Muslims, unarmed Muslims, both, or neither? Do you remember exactly what you said in that regard?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said it was -- it would apply to anybody that remained in the -- in the pocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Thayer asked the witness for her opinion, and the witness said in her answer "I believe." I think this is irrelevant for the establishment of facts. The witness was asked about this issue in cross-examination as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. And this is perhaps the reason why Mr. Thayer is dealing with this part. The witness was not asked for her opinion. Mr. Thayer asked her: "Do you recall exactly what you said with respect to whether liquidation would apply to armed Muslims ..." And then later, in the second part of the question: "Do you remember exactly what you said in this regard?" This is it not a question with which he asked for an opinion. Please carry on, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And why don't we --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the interpretation we received was "what do you think about," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That might be an interpretation issue but I heard it as I read it to you, and that is recorded in that way. Thank you very much. Please continue, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to ask you a question, ma'am, that ties into two topics about which General Tolimir cross-examined you. He put it to you at one point, or he asked you, whether the fear of the Bosniaks in Zepa was justified and whether it ever materialised. I think he asked that just before the break. Do you recall that question or those two questions, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to show you a document which will address that question and I think also tie into another topic that General Tolimir raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have P00755 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We can stay on the first page in the English because we can see from the original which is next to it that this is type-signed by Commander Rajko Kusic, the commander of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade, also known as the Rogatica Brigade. Did you ever have occasion to meet him or hear about him during your time in Zepa, Colonel Kusic?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have heard his name, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall ever meeting him?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that he was among the Bosnian Serb military who -- officers who were part of General Mladic's company. But we were never -- I was never personally introduced to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand you never had the pleasure of his introduction. If we look at the date, it's 8 August 1995. We can see that it is a daily combat report to the Drina Corps Command. It refers specifically to events, as we can see, that occurred on the 7th of August, 1995, in the afternoon. There's a reference here to the canyon of the Praca river and five remaining -- and Colonel Kusic uses the derogatory term "Balija" who were, after the fall of Zepa, travelling along a certain route. And he indicates that they went down to the railroad tracks at Dub and tried to reach Renovica walking on the railroad tracks and that this group was liquidated. He goes on to say that the group was separate and it travelled for ten days. And I'd ask you, if you could look at the original, do you see the portion where it says, "the group was separate and it travelled for ten days"? Do you see that in the original Serbian, or B/C/S, as we call it here?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I do see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. We have the English translation here and I'll just read up to a point. It says: "The same day, in the vicinity of Luke, an unarmed Ustasha, borne in Srebrenica, 24 years old," and we can see how it's been translated. I want to ask you, can you see what word is actually used here in the original?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It -- the word used is - my pronunciation is bad, I apologise - "likvidiran."

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. And is that the same verb that General Mladic used in that encounter that you were asked so many questions about?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The report goes on, and it says: "Before he died," referring to this unarmed man, "he said that he fell behind the others and he was looking for ... food." My question to you, ma'am, is: From what you can see here in this report, how does the fate of this young unarmed hungry man correspond to the fears that you personally saw expressed during your time in Zepa by the Bosniak population?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would appear to bear out their justifiable fears, the Bosnian Muslim's justifiable fears of what would happen after the deadline had passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I object to the question because the Prosecutor put the question without knowing how the soldier perished. Was it after the fighting for the enclave of Zepa or whether it was at some other front. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer was reading from the text in front of us. Mr. Thayer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, that concludes my re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Mindua has a question for the witness. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness. Good afternoon, first of all. I would like to ask you the following. Actually, I have two questions for you. But before I put these questions, I would just like to remind you, of course, not to hesitate to let me know if I misunderstood what you said. I do not want to take up any time in order to look for the exact reference on the transcript, but I believe you said with respect to the letter of Colonel Avdo Palic who sent therefore that letter to President Alija Izetbegovic as being a letter which was a desperate call, and this is something that you mentioned when you talked about the evacuation by helicopter of the men from Zepa. So this was my first observation. Second observation is that you said today as well that General Smith did not believe that General Mladic would accept the evacuation of the men from Zepa by helicopter. So, as I mentioned that I had two questions for you, I will now put the first question. So do you know what made General Smith say that, when he said that General Mladic would never accept the evacuation by helicopter of the men from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the evacuation by helicopter was first raised by Mr. Torlak, General Mladic was party to that conversation between Mr. Torlak and General Smith. And my recollection is that General Mladic indicated that he would not -- that this would not be an acceptable resolution, to evacuate the men of fighting age by helicopter, and he kept referring to all of the buses and road transportation that the Bosnian Serb army had organised for the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. Now I have a second question for you. I wanted to know if the UNPROFOR was charging their services in case of helicopter evacuations, so I wanted to ask you the question, before you actually said that Mr. Torlak -- or that, rather, General Mladic, had already said and expressed his hesitance in terms of that type of transportation to Mr. Torlak, so I would like to know if Colonel Avdo Palic knew that General Mladic would not pay or would not allow for or does not support this helicopter evacuation of the men from Zepa, do you know why did Colonel Avdo Palic ask President Izetbegovic if he was willing to pay for transportation fees and to charge them to the UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I do not know why Colonel Palic believed that UNPROFOR would charge a fee to be -- to arrange the evacuation by helicopter. At none of the meetings that I was present at was any form of payment for UNPROFOR discussed, in terms of helicopter evacuation or road evacuation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Judge Nyambe has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you. Just to follow up on Judge Mindua's question, the issue of who would pay for the evacuation if it was undertaken by helicopter did arise in some of the -- in one of the documents that was presented today to Court, if my memory serves me right. Do you agree that it has -- let me rephrase my question. Do you agree that it was raised?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- the document that we saw, the telegram from Colonel Palic to President Izetbegovic, I believe that's where there is a question about whether the Bosnian government would pay UNPROFOR. And I don't recall at any of the meetings where I was present there being any notion of UNPROFOR charging anybody for evacuation by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: My question is: Which came first? The telegram to the president about the cost, if it -- the cost of the evacuation if it was under taken by helicopter; or General Mladic's use of the term liquidate, liquidate them? Which came first?

utterances.speaker: EMMA SAYER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't recall the date of Mr. Palic's telegram to the Presidency. But I do -- can speak to the meeting at the Presidency in the late hours of the 25th of July and the early hours of the 26th, where Minister Muratovic was very insistent that the evacuation of the population of Zepa should be by helicopter. So that was certainly mentioned by the Bosnian Presidency side at that meeting and is memorialised in my note of that meeting. My recollection of the term "liquidate" is at -- is memorialised in the meeting note, the summary, as at 0800 on the 28th of July, I believe. But perhaps it might be helpful to -- to check that on -- on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I may be able to save us some time. The reference to the telegram from Colonel Palic to President Izetbegovic, which General Tolimir used during his cross, is at paragraph 110 of D55, and the report indicates that telegram was at 0700 on the 27th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Ms. Sayer, you will be pleased to hear that this concludes your examination in this trial. Thank you very much that you came to The Hague and provided us with your knowledge and memory. Now you are free to return to your normal activities. The Chamber would like to thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think we have not only reached the time of the end of today's hearing but we are over time now. We can't start with the next witness, although Mr. Elderkin entered the courtroom. We have to adjourn and resume tomorrow at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
